source.version_note: Frontiers in Psychology 13:1052729, published 4 January 2023. DOI contains 2022 and manuscript was accepted in November 2022; the published citation year is explicitly 2023.
source.verification_method: All supplied pages read, including two experiment designs, full instructions, statistics, limitations and references.

citation.title: Humans, machines, and double standards? The moral evaluation of the actions of autonomous vehicles, anthropomorphized autonomous vehicles, and human drivers in road-accident dilemmas

reading.source_scope_note: Two human online experiments rating completed hypothetical road-accident actions. Agent descriptions and vehicle naming vary; actual driving, safety, blame, deployment acceptance, mental-state mediation and memory performance are not measured.
access_limits: All 13 supplied pages read. Numerical and plotted patterns are described in the extracted results/captions; no independent raw-data analysis performed.
OSF data, code and dissertation were not independently inspected. Primary animacy-memory, attention and anthropomorphism studies cited in the background remain unread.

study.experiment_1: 444 start, 79 incomplete and five eligibility exclusions, leaving 360 adults (266 women/94 men, age 18–80). Random human-driver N=187 or AV N=173; German online sample with student credit or voucher lottery.
study.experiment_2: 892 start; 80 incomplete, ten ineligible, 37 withdrawal/display issues and ten double-participation exclusions leave 755 (317 women/437 men/one diverse; age 18–87). Human N=248, named AV N=250, ordinary AV N=257. Commercial German panel.
study.design: Between-person agent; within-person sacrifice occupant versus pedestrians and one/two/five pedestrians. Each of six combinations repeated four times, 24 judgments per person; side counterbalanced and trial order randomized. Six-point action rating from very reprehensible to very justifiable.
study.manipulation: Named AV introduced as an intelligent driving system called Alina, subsequently referred to by name. This bundles name and mentalistic description; no direct human-likeness or inferred-mind manipulation check isolates the mechanism.
study.analysis: Multivariate repeated-measures analysis without sphericity requirement; Holm-adjusted post-hoc comparisons. Failed attention-check participants retained after disclosed sensitivity checks show unchanged statistical conclusions.
study.results: Experiment 1 mean human rating 3.64 versus AV 3.18, agent partial eta-squared .10. Experiment 2 human 3.39, named AV 3.11, ordinary AV 2.86; named-versus-ordinary F=11.35, p=.001. More lives saved improves ratings across agents. Small experiment-1 interactions do not replicate in experiment 2.
study.interpretation: Descriptive human advantage and a naming/description effect on action approval, not proof of an irrational double standard, increased actual safety or shared underlying moral processes.

summary: Add the explicitly secondary animacy memory advantage, with task-specific boundaries from the cited titles. Extend existing anthropomorphism and human–robot moral-evaluation evidence. Distinguish the replicated agent rating difference from small unreplicated interactions, causal mental-state stories and recommendations to market systems as more human.

findings.definition: Better memory for information about living entities than for comparable inanimate entities, especially in free-recall tasks.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary background pattern in a fully read moral-evaluation paper; this study does not measure memory or establish an AI analogue
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether a system disproportionately retains or retrieves information about people or animals relative to matched objects in tasks where equal recall matters. Control frequency, relevance, emotional salience, lexical properties and exposure; do not infer human episodic memory or an evolved mechanism from output differences.
findings.novelty_rationale: Content-dependent memory advantage differs from general salience, memory for self-relevant items, anthropomorphic attribution and preference in moral evaluation. Attention to animacy is related but not assumed to be the same mechanism.

evidence.quote: prioritization of humans and animals over inanimate objects in
memory and attention in recent years

findings.evidence_scope: Introduction explicitly summarizes animate-over-inanimate prioritization in memory and attention. The bibliography identifies a task distinction—free recall enhanced but cued recall impaired—and competing mechanism papers. These titles refine scope, not independently verify those primary outcomes. Current experiments only measure moral ratings.
findings.boundary: The advantage is task-dependent, not every memory measure or every living stimulus. Naming a machine need not make it alive or improve its memory. Evolution, arousal, semantic richness and category strategies are alternative accounts, not mechanisms identified in this supplied study. No additional primary full readings are claimed.

findings.definition: Comparable completed road-accident actions receive more favorable moral ratings when attributed to a human driver than an autonomous vehicle.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing agent-dependent evaluation pattern, now with two experiments within one additional fully read article; do not count them as two independent papers.

evaluation of the agent itself or questions of blame and responsibility

findings.evidence_scope: Human-versus-AV action-approval differences replicate across two samples. Both sources are rated more favorably when fewer die. Small agent-by-action/number interactions from experiment 1 are undetected in experiment 2; this is not an equivalence test or proof of identical moral principles.
findings.boundary: Action approval, actor suitability, blame, responsibility, outrage and actual technology use are distinct. Comparing human self-sacrifice with a vehicle sacrificing its passenger includes different agent–victim relationships. Relevant perceived duties or capacities may justify different judgments; a difference is not automatically irrational prejudice.

findings.term: Anthropomorphizing a vehicle changes action evaluation
findings.definition: A first name and intelligent-agent description are used to make an autonomous vehicle more human-like, accompanying more favorable ratings of its actions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing human-attribution concept; no new Alina effect or independent mechanism is invented from this specific naming intervention.

findings.evidence_scope: Experiment 2 contrasts named/mentalistically described AV versus ordinary AV with identical hypothetical actions. Mean action rating improves from 2.86 to 3.11. No direct attribution, expectation, trust, safety or blame mediator is measured; authors explicitly leave the exact cognition unresolved.
findings.boundary: Human-like framing can influence evaluation without increasing actual capability, safety or moral agency. Greater acceptance is not inherently beneficial and is not evidence that concealment or misleading personification is justified. Naming, familiarity, gender cues and intelligent-system wording are not separately isolated.

methodological_limits: The article is published in January 2023 despite 2022 in its DOI/volume context. Use the explicit publication year rather than infer year from DOI digits.

Both experiments rate completed hypothetical actions; they do not ask participants to choose an action themselves or measure actual adoption, willingness to ride, crash behavior, casualties or liability. The authors explicitly distinguish action evaluation from blame/responsibility.

The human driver is the person sacrificed in the occupant-loss condition, whereas the vehicle sacrifices a passenger. Identical casualty counts do not make every duty, relationship or perceived responsibility identical.

The anthropomorphism intervention bundles first name, reference style and intelligent-driving-system description. No direct human-likeness, inferred-mind, perceived-gender or expectation measure distinguishes the proposed mediators.

The reported human contrast in experiment 2 compares human versus both vehicle conditions together; the named-versus-ordinary contrast is separately tested. Do not label every individual scenario-level ordering or every unreported human-versus-named contrast as a separately significant test.

Experiment-1 interactions are small and fail to replicate in the larger second experiment. This supports caution about those moderators but is not a formal equivalence test showing no smaller interaction or identical psychological rules.

Potential ceiling compression of favorable human self-sacrifice ratings can affect observed interactions. A null interaction alone cannot discriminate a general evaluation shift from all alternative models of moral principles.

The two samples differ in recruitment, age and gender composition. Replication across them supports robustness of the main contrast, but sample differences cannot identify age, gender or experience as causal moderators.
Sensitivity power calculations approximate a reduced design and correlations. They do not establish every subgroup or interaction has the same power. The article discloses this approximation.

Four repeated presentations of six scenarios yield 24 ratings per participant, not 24 independent moral cases or 24 independent people. Within-person dependence is addressed by the repeated-measures design; repeated-case generalization remains limited.

Abstract newspaper-like scenarios and one six-point evaluation scale cannot establish how directly affected people respond, whether all news framings behave similarly or what real institutions should decide.

The authors' prediction that anthropomorphism may reduce adverse public response is a proposed application. Improved approval does not verify safety, appropriate trust, ethical acceptability or informed public consent.

The initial animacy discussion is background from other work, not an experiment in memory or attention here. Primary references identify competing explanations and task differences; no unified animate-priority mechanism is established.

Moral theories are broader than a single casualty count or action. Saving more lives is not the only relevant moral criterion, and a named machine does not thereby acquire human feelings, rights or full moral responsibility.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Adds another agent-asymmetry context, but its action-approval ratings should not be merged with the earlier moral-agent duty/suitability outcomes as though they were a single scale.
Both studies vary human versus artificial actors, but a naming manipulation and completed crash evaluation differ from medication refusal, coercion and outcome-based judgment.

The low-stakes nursing null does not negate this vehicle evaluation effect, and this vehicle result does not prove stakes causally explain that null. Different samples, roles, outcomes and human-like manipulations remain.

Mayer's earlier self-protection paper concerns imagined personal choices and indirect elicitation; the present article concerns observer evaluations. Shared authors and topic do not make these duplicate studies, nor do they establish the same self-protection mechanism.

deferred.reason: Already covered by human–robot moral judgment asymmetry; the specific negative-AV direction does not warrant a second near-synonymous entry.
Related background is explicit, but primary task definitions and attention mechanisms require reading the cited originals. Do not infer that attention and memory have one identified mechanism.
Blame, culpability, liability and intervention opportunities are not measured; the action-rating effect is insufficient.

limitations: One secondary memory concept and two existing empirical evidence notes. No new ethical-violation or harm edges, legal findings or safe-driving recommendations are inferred.
